en: One thing you'll note when defining custom
skills
is that you'll end up with a bunch of new
slash commands.
In Claude Code, when you type a forward
slash in that command prompt here,
you got a couple of built-in and also custom
slash commands to choose from. The idea
behind all the commands you see here, no
matter if they're custom or built-in, is
that they give you quick access to certain
extra features. And you already saw some
built-in commands like the init command
already, for example.
The config command allows you to view and
tweak the configuration. The clear command
clears the context. You saw all that. But
your skills will also show up as commands
here. For example, I got a modern accessible
HTML JSX command in there because I got an
equally named skill in this project.
But what's the idea behind that? Well, the
primary use case of these skills is that
Claude Code can discover and use them as
needed depending on the task it's working
on. So the primary use case of these skills
is not that you invoke them, but you could
invoke them. You could invoke your skills as
commands, but of course it will then depend
on what's inside the skill definition
markdown document what will happen. And if
it's just a bunch of extra knowledge, like
with the skills I shared with you,
nothing will really happen. If I execute
this Bun instead of Node skill here,
you'll see that Claude Code starts working,
but it'll get back to me that it doesn't
really know what to do. Because in that
skill, I just share some general knowledge
about Bun and that we're using Bun instead
of Node.js, for example, but I don't tell it
what to do. However, you could of course
build skills
that do have extra instructions or maybe
even scripts attached to them. That is
something you can do. And in such
situations, you might occasionally wanna
invoke them as custom commands. That's why
this feature exists here.
However, the primary use case of skills is
that Claude discovers and uses them and
we'll later dive into building custom
commands that are primarily meant for
execution by you instead.
